newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians battle deadly Mekong River flooding.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians battle deadly Mekong River flooding.

text.p: Flood waters from the rain-swollen Mekong River have killed at least five people in Cambodia, forced tens of thousands to flee their homes and submerged thousands of hectares (acres) of crops.
As they counted the cost, Cambodian leaders appealed on Monday for flood relief and said the death toll could rise.

"This is a terrible disaster... We should request the local and international Red Cross to help the flood victims," First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said in Kompong Cham, flooded capital of Cambodia's most populous province.
The flooding has hit four provinces stretching hundreds of kilometres (miles) from the border with Laos to Phnom Penh.
Information Ministry spokesman Sieng Lapresse said disaster officials said at least five people drowned in Kratie province and believed there might be more deaths.

Agriculture Minister Tao Seng Huor told Reuters in this eastern town on the Mekong more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of paddy had flooded and tens of thousands of people were homeless. He spoke of some fatalities, but had no figure.

Hun Neng, governor of Kompong Cham, said 30 percent of the province's 1.5 million people were affected by flooding that damaged large areas of paddy. The province produces about 10 percent of the country's annual rice output.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, brother of the Kompong Cham governor, flew over flooded areas on Sunday and declared a state of emergency in the province.
"The floods this year are very barbarous and cause suffering to people living in the Mekong River basin. Although we don't have many people dead, it has destroyed houses, property," he said.
The centre of Kompong Cham was flooded on Monday, with people wading knee-deep through water and others seen moving food stocks to upper floors of their houses.
The central market was shut after flooding, but a few people tried to sell goods from boats, a witness said.

Officials said it was too early to tell how crops were affected. "The price of rice has gone up slightly, but not a strong increase," said an Agriculture Ministry official on Monday. "Before the flood, there was a good outlook for the rice crop, but now it is not clear."
Cambodia was hit by damaging floods in 1991. Two years ago floods followed by drought hit rice output and caused severe hardship for many rural families.
Last year was a bumper harvest. Cambodia was self sufficient in rice and had modest exports for the first time in over 20 years.
